title: The body scan in the rule

hook: a weekly scan: Moses answered here am I at the burning bush, and the first thing asked of him was his shoes

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: breathe. Palamas let the breath gather the mind, and Barlaam warned it isn't the goal. Today, the whole body gets a turn, starting with the feet.

Step out of your shoes at someone's door and the floor suddenly has a temperature: cool tile, a soft rug, the grain of a wooden board. Moses was keeping his father-in-law's sheep far out in the desert, at Horeb, when he saw a bush on fire that wasn't burning up. He turned aside to look. And a voice called him from the middle of the bush: Moses, Moses.
screen: `THE FLOOR UNDER BARE FEET.` → `A BUSH THAT DOESN'T BURN UP.` → `HE TURNS ASIDE TO LOOK.` → `MOSES, MOSES.`

segments.voice: He answered: "Here am I." In Hebrew, it's one word: hineni. It's the same word the boy Samuel said in the night. It isn't a question back, like what do you want. It's how people in the Hebrew Bible answer a call: ready, and here. And then, before any message, before the name of God, before the mission to Egypt, the voice asks something of his body: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Presence starts at the soles of the feet. Jewish practice has its own bare-feet moment. The Talmud records a rule that the priests don't go up to give the priestly blessing in their sandals, and in synagogues where the kohanim still bless the congregation, they take off their shoes first. The rabbis give their own reasons for it, but the picture rhymes with the bush. Notice what changed at the bush. The ground under Moses had been there all along. He turned aside, answered, and felt it under his feet. Here's where it meets the body scan. A scan is hineni given part by part, starting where Moses started: the feet on the ground. Then the legs, the belly, the hands, the tight jaw, the tired back. Each one gets the same answer: here. Not fixed yet, not judged. Just met. A weekly scan in your rule is a standing appointment to take your shoes off and notice the ground you've been standing on all week.
screen: `HINENI: READY, AND HERE.` · `PUT OFF THY SHOES FROM OFF THY FEET.` · `HOLY GROUND.` · `FEET: HERE. HANDS: HERE.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Take off your shoes if you can, and set your bare feet flat on the floor. Feel the ground first: cool or warm, hard or soft. Then move your attention slowly upward: legs, belly, hands, shoulders, jaw, the top of your head. At each place, answer silently: here. If a place is tight or sore, don't fix it yet. Just answer it.
The body scan in the rule: a weekly scan, from the feet up, answering here I am, the way Moses answered at the bush.

howItsDone: Body scans, moving attention slowly through the body, are used in Buddhist-rooted and secular meditation. Hineni, here I am, is the Hebrew Bible's answer to a call, and kohanim take off their shoes before giving the priestly blessing.

fork.reveal: The ground under Moses was holy before anything was asked of him. A scan answers hineni to the body as it is, starting from the feet.
